## **How to disguise evolutionary traps created by solar panels**

## **Theodore V. Black[1] · Bruce A. Robertson[1]**

Received: 23 July 2019 / Accepted: 29 October 2019 © Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2019

## **Abstract**

Photovoltaic panels are the most rapidly growing source of sustainable energy, but are also sources of polarized light pollution that can mislead aquatic insects into thinking they represent natural waterbodies. Aquatic insects are commonly attracted away from natural water bodies to lay their eggs upon solar panels where they fail to hatch, a phenomenon called an evolutionary trap. Previous work demonstrates that the addition of white, non-polarizing gridding with 2–20 mm line width to solar panels can effectively ‘disarm’ this type of evolutionary trap, rendering it less attractive to three families of aquatic insects. However, the geographic and taxonomic breadth of the efficacy may be limited, and the economic cost associated with reducing the black solar-active area of solar panels has not yet been quantified. We designed a field experiment to test whether line width or density is more important in reducing the maladaptive attraction of aquatic insects to simulated solar panels, and expanded the geographic and taxonomic breadth of testing this approach to disarming evolutionary traps. We found that line width could be manipulated to strongly reduce attraction by all taxa. The effective line width was between 1 and 5 mm, indicating that solar panel-induced evolutionary traps can be disarmed with a more modest reduction in solaractive area than was previously assumed. Interruption of attraction through the addition of non-polarizing surface patterns appears to be a fundamental aspect of aquatic insect interpretation of environmental polarized light signals that can be used to disguise evolutionary traps.

**Keywords** Ecological trap · Aquatic insect · Photovoltaic · Solar energy · Maladaptation · Conservation behavior

## **Introduction**

Evolutionary traps are scenarios in which animals are fooled by rapidly changing conditions into preferring poor-quality resources over those that are superior in terms of survival or reproduction (Schlaepfer et al. 2002). They occur because the environmental cues that animals have evolved to inform their decision-making are no longer reliable and actually lead to the most fitness-negative behavioral option available (Robertson et al. 2013). Animals come to prefer inferior mates, foods, habitats, nest sites or other resources. Evolutionary traps result in rapid population declines (Fletcher et al. 2012) and have recently helped explain continent-wide declines in European honey bees ( _Apis mellifera_ : Kessler et al. 2015; Rundlöf et al. 2015 ), and monarch butterflies ( _Danaus plexippus_ : Faldyn et al. 2018), and led to the

> * Bruce A. Robertson broberts@bard.edu

extirpation of a population of Edith’s checkerspot butterfly ( _Euphydryas editha_ : Singer and Parmesan 2018) and the _Acan-_ near extinction of Be’er Sheva fringe-fingered lizard ( _thodactylus beershebensis_ : Hawlena et al. 2010). A disproportionately high fraction of globally endangered species have at least one of their populations caught in an evolutionary trap, indicating that traps are a key consideration in efforts to stabilize populations and prevent species extinctions (Robertson and Blumstein 2019).

The most well-understood example of an evolutionary trap occurs when smooth, dark-colored man-made objects (e.g. asphalt: Kriska et al. 1998; glass buildings: Kriska et al. 2008 ), strongly and horizontally polarize reflected sunlight, mimicking the environmental cue most aquatic insects rely upon to identify waterbodies suitable for oviposition (reviewed in Horváth and Varjú 2004). Artificial polarizers can polarize light to a greater degree (90–100%) than any natural water body ( _d_ ≈ 30–80%, Horváth and Varjú 2004) and water-seeking aquatic insects are preferentially attracted to oviposit upon these supernormally polarized light sources

where their eggs fail to hatch (Kriska et al. 1998, 2008; Horváth et al. 2010).

Solar panels have been identified as a strong source of polarized light pollution (Horváth et al. 2009, 2010) which have the potential to attract aquatic insects away from their natural habitats and contribute to declines in their populations on a global scale. The ecological impact of solar panels should expand in tandem with global-scale growth photovoltaic (PV) power capacity which is growing exponentially and has increased by 45% since 2016 (International Energy Agency 2019). Research investigating the impacts of utility scale and residential PV production on ecological interactions and species persistence is very limited, but utility-scale PV facilities are already known to have a range of harmful ecological impacts (reviewed in Lovich and Ennen 2011; Jeal et al. 2019) and there is a pressing need to identify ways to resolve PV power generation with ecological conservation.

Horváth et al. (2010 ) identified one such mitigating strategy. Commercial solar panels are not solid shiny black surfaces, but various models contain a diversity of configurations of white lines and spaces between and within the power generating PV cells. Horváth et al. (2010) demonstrated that the addition of thick, white, non-polarized gridding to simulated solar panels has the ability to dramatically (10–26-fold) reduce the attractiveness of the panels to three families of aquatic insect families in central Europe. This suggests that it is possible to create particular solar panel designs that reflect light with high degrees of polarization, but which nevertheless fail to attract all water-seeking insects due to the configuration of their polarizing- and non-polarizing surface colors and textures. Yet, the mechanism by which white gridding effectively ‘disguises’ these evolutionary traps has remained unclear. And because the extent of white gridding reduces solar-active area, eliminating traps via this method must come at a cost in energy production that requires minimization. Quantification of these trade-offs would provide insight into the economic feasibility of this approach to attenuating the impacts of evolutionary traps. Finally, if the integration of white gridding patterns into PV panel manufacture are worth pursuing to help achieve conservation and management goals, it is important to know if gridding is effective for more than the relative few taxa that have been tested (Horváth et al. 2010 ), and that the effective reduction in attractiveness is sufficiently strong to justify additional attention.

We designed a field choice experiment to test if the density of gridding or the width of individual grid lines were more important in reducing the attractiveness of polarized light sources to four taxonomic groups of aquatic insects. This study was conducted on a different continent than previous work, and investigated the behavioral responses of two broad taxonomic groups known from previous work

to experience reduced attraction to polarized light sources associated with 10–20 mm wide white gridding (caddisflies (tricoptera) and mayflies (ephemeroptera); Horváth et al. 2010) and two insect families whose responses to gridding have never been tested: midges (chironomidae) and black flies (simuliidae). We simulated the polarization profiles of horizontally oriented solar panels using oil-filled trays painted with four patterns of white gridding, plus one solid black control, and exposed these test surfaces to four taxonomic groups of free-flying emergent aquatic insect in the process of selecting oviposition sites. We interpret lower individual captures in experimental treatments relative to the solid black control in terms of reduced attractiveness. Finally, we examined variation amongst taxa in how strongly their attraction to simulated solar panels declined with the reductions of solar active area resulting from the inclusion of various gridding patterns.

## **Materials and methods**

We selected a study site on the heavily forested and lightly populated Saw Kill River, New York, U.S.A. The experiment was placed on an ornamental lawn extending from 3 to 30 m from the water, to ensure insect lines of sight and movement toward experimental test surfaces. Insects were trapped five times between July 24 and September 9, 2015 on days with clear skies from 1900 to 2100 h. We focused on obtaining higher experimental replication at a single study site rather than fewer replicates at many study sites because we were more interested in detecting behavioral responses to our experimental treatments rather than expanding the spatial scope of inference of those responses.

We exposed insects to five reflection-polarization patterns represented by painted, oil-filled (depth 0.5 cm) plastic trays (65 × 45 × 2 cm), each painted with a different configuration of non-polarizing white-gridding on a solid black background (Fig. 1). Gridding patterns created equal-sized rectangles that would strongly polarize only the skylight reflecting from the oil surface directly above the black portions. Trays were spaced 45 cm apart, five meters from the water in a row parallel to the direction of flow of the river along their long axis. On each trap night the tray’s position in relation to the stream was rotated every 24 min so that each experimental treatment had equal time in each of the five trapping stations. We changed the starting location for the tray’s rotation order on each subsequent trap night. We poured the contents of each tray through fine cheesecloth to separate insects, which we then stored in 80% ethanol for later identification. We focused our analysis on four groups of aquatic insect known to exhibit stronger attraction to sources of horizontally polarized light with greater degrees (percentages) of polarization: Ephemeroptera (Kriska et al.

1998, 2006), trichoptera (Kriska et al. 2008; Horváth et al. 2010), simuliidae (Robertson et al. 2018), and chironomidae (Lerner et al. 2008; Horváth et al. 2011; Robertson et al. 2018). When seeking a suitable oviposition site, these taxa touchdown on the surface of water bodies (Kriska et al. 2006; reviewed in Horváth and Varjú 2004), but will be captured in the oil-traps.

We measured the reflection-polarization characteristics of oil-filled trays using imaging polarimetry (Horváth and Varjú 2004) on a cloud-free day. Our polarimeter was a Canon EOS Rebel T6 DSLR camera aimed downward at the oil-filled trays at the Brewster’s angle θBrewster = arctan (refractive index of oil = 1.5) = 56.3° from the vertical which results in the highest possible degree of polarization. Three images were taken of each object with the polarization filter at different angles, then processed via Polarworks© software into images illustrating the degree ( _d_ ) and angle (α) of polarization at each pixel (Fig. 1).

We examined the effect of gridding treatment on the captures of four focal taxonomic groups of aquatic insects. We created a standardized abundance metric reflective of the relative fraction of individuals attracted to each treatment to avoid bias associated with disproportionately high or low captures during any one capture session. We divided the

total number of captures per square cm of black, polarizing and solar/active area for each tray, and adjusted estimates upward to standardize measurements for a 200 cm[2] area. Captures per treatment were converted to a fraction of the total number of captures for that visit at that site, then multiplied by 100 and rounded to the nearest whole individual. We modeled standardized captures using generalized linear models with a log-link function and fit models to negative binomial or Poisson distributions suitable for count data. Finally, we calculated the reductions of black reflective area relative to controls in each treatment in our study and in Horvath et al.’s (2010) study and plotted those against the reductions of captures in that treatment relative to controls.

## **Results**

We captured a total of 10,986 adult water-seeking aquatic insects in four taxonomic groups: chironomidae = 10,102 (91.9%); simuliidae = 556 (5.0%); trichoptera = 181 (1.6%); ephemeroptera = 147 (1.3%). Poisson distributions best fit the data for chironomid and ephemeroptera data, while simuliid and trichoptera captures best fit negative binomial distributions (all ĉ = 1.2–3.7). Captures of all four taxa were

highest in the black and 6L thin trays, which insects did not distinguish between (chironomidae: χ[2] = 271.8, df = 4, P < 0.0001; trichoptera: χ[2] = 38.4, df = 4, P < 0.0001; simuliidae: χ[2] = 23.3, df = 4, P = 0.0001; ephemeroptera: χ[2] = 17.0, df = 4, P < 0.002, Fig. 2). The attractiveness of the next most attractive reflection-polarization treatment, 6L med, fell off by 32.2% in chironomids, 29.2% in black flies, 34.0% in caddisflies and 12.6% in mayflies (Fig. 2). Captures of the two remaining treatments, 4L thick and 6L thick were lowest in all four taxa. We found reductions in captures associated with gridding patterns to be a function of increasing area of white non-polarizing stripes, with the maximum reduction for all four taxa occurring in the transition from 1.1 to 5.5% reduction in black simulated solar-active area (Fig. 3). Black portions of trays polarized a higher fraction of reflected sunlight ( _d_ black = 53–88%), relative to the whitegridding ( _d_ white = 23–38%, Fig. 1b) and did so in a horizontal direction (Fig. 1c).

Treatments in our study reduced the black surface area of test surfaces in our study by 0.05% (6L thin), 2.28% (6L medium), 4.32% (4L thick), and 5.68% (6L thick), and in Horvath et al.’s (2010) treatments by 0.99% (n = 2 lines), 2.9% (n = 6 lines) and 4.74% (n = 10 lines) relative to controls. Plotting reductions in captures vs. reduction in black area for resulted in a similar patterns of trade-offs among aquatic insects, with ephemeroptera from our study sites in

New York experiencing a more muted reduction in attraction in response to gridding patterns (Fig. 3).

## **Discussion**

We found that the manipulating the width of non-polarizing white gridding was highly effective in reducing the attractiveness of simulated horizontally-oriented solar panels to four groups of water-seeking aquatic insects, that relatively thin grid-lines were effective in this manner, and that manipulating line width can be more effective than reducing line density. Even the addition of grid lines of relatively small width (between 1 and 5 mm) reduced the relative attractiveness of our very strongly and horizontally polarizing surfaces above 80% for most taxa with only a 2–3% reduction in solar-active area. This indicates a large diversity of extant and potential photovoltaic panel designs exist that are capable of minimizing the trade-off between energy production and ecological impact mitigation for a broad taxaonomic group of aquatic insects. In addition, this study confirms previous work demonstrating that white partitions are effective tools in reducing the strength of polarized light-based evolutionary traps created by solar panels (Horváth et al. 2010), on another continent, and for two additional families of aquatic insects (chrionomidae, simuliidae).

The four aquatic insect groups we examined in this study responded similarly to experimental manipulations. Reductions in attraction to simulated solar panels occurred with the inclusion of lines that were between 1 and 5 mm in width, were similar or marginally greater when doubling line width to 10 mm, and were unrelated to a modest increase in line density. Horváth et al.’s (2010) study used larger 2 m × 2 m panels compared to our 0.65 m × 0.45 m trays, and used a broader array of non-polarizing line densities: 2, 6 and 10 per treatment. Their most highly gridded treatment (n = 10) led to a 94–99% reduction in captures of dolichopodids, ephemeroptera and trichoptera relative to ungridded controls. We found that we could reduce attraction by similar amounts in trichoptera (caddisflies), chironomids (midges), and simuliids (black flies) by using lines that were 50–90% thinner. Alone, this might suggest that gridding of any density might be much thinner and remain effective as an attraction mitigation approach. However, when plotting reductions in captures of our treatments and that of Horváth et al. (2010) together with an axis representing the percentage of black, potentially solar-active area lost to gridding, 3). the trade-off curves appear similar for most groups (Fig. This suggests that neither line density nor line width, specifically, may be the critical factor in dissuading aquatic insects from ovipositing on solar panels.

Aquatic insects are known to have increasing preferences for surfaces of progressively darker colors that polarize increasingly higher percentages of polarized light (Robertson et al. 2018). In a similar way, Fig. 3 suggests that

insects may be more attracted to surfaces that polarize a higher average fraction of polarized light across a particular area, regardless of the configuration or pattern of that light within the boundaries of the surface. In other words, individual insects may ‘visually average’ the relative amount of non-polarizing versus polarizing area within some specific field of view or they may be even using specific combinations of polarized and non-polarized signals to inform oviposition behavior. Because turbid flowing water in rapids or waterfalls polarize less light (Horváth and Varjú 2004 such a behavioral rule could serve as a mechanism by which aquatic insects gather more detailed information on the hydrological properties of potential oviposition sites. Darker, more nutrient rich waters also polarize more light and so this same rule would generally guide insects to more suitable habitat. Alternatively, avoidance of gridded polarized light sources could be a product of selection to avoid small habitat patches. If this were true, the variable responses to grid line thickness could be a result of the taxon-specific ability of compound insect eyes to sufficiently resolve thin non-polarizing partitions (Horváth et al. 2010). The details of the mechanism underlying the effect of white gridding in reducing attractiveness to aquatic insects remains unknown.

If avoidance of fragmented patches of habitat underlie reductions in attraction, this won’t affect the quantitative calibration of our study with that of Horváth et al.’s (2010 because we fragmented our panels in comparable ways and reductions were compared to unfragmented panels. It could, however, mean that larger solar panels will have a higher

absolute attractiveness than smaller ones, though reductions associated with white gridding will be proportional. Because our study and that of Horváth et al.’s (2010) simulated the visual-polarization properties of solar panels using different methods (e.g. paraffin coated black plastic vs. oilfilled painted plastic trays), future studies should evaluate if insects perceive these surfaces differently and/or calibrate their work these studies carefully.

Extant and commercially available PV panel designs represent an incredibly diverse array of configurations of solar-active (light polarizing) and white (non-polarizing) surfaces. Our results indicate significant flexibility exists in the placement and width of non-polarizing stripping on solar panels that disguise evolutionary traps, though no research investigates a potential role for pattern in the efficacy of disguising these traps. This suggests that any constraints in the configuration of white-gridding on panels inherent to the design and manufacturing of solar panels may not act as important constraints on future designs that act to reduce their attractiveness to aquatic insects. Importantly, we also demonstrate that line width can act as a break point at which highly regular patterns of non-polarized signals go ignored or undetected and the trap becomes ‘active’ again. Antireflective coatings that increase the efficiency of PV panels while reducing their ability to polarize reflected sunlight are an alternative to white gridding, but at least one technology appears to be a relatively ineffective alternative, leading to a major reduction, (Tabanidae), no reduction (Chironomidae) reduction, or even a fourfold increase in attraction relative to solid continuously polarizing surface controls (Száz et al. 2016).

This study demonstrates that interruption of attraction through the addition of non-polarizing surface patterns is a fundamental aspect of aquatic insect interpretation of environmental polarized light signals that can be used to disguise environmental cues that normally trigger evolutionary traps. The development of this technique for eliminating evolutionary traps is in its infancy (reviewed in Robertson and Blumstein 2019) and this polarized light-aquatic insect system represents a powerful first model system for developing it. An essential pre-requisite to disarming evolutionary traps is a deep understanding of the sensory, cognitive and behavioral mechanisms that guide behaviors under trap and nontrap conditions (Robertson et al. 2013; Greggor et al. 2014; Robertson and Chalfoun 2016). The underlying mechanisms in this system remain elusive, but we recommend testing the ‘visual averaging’ hypotheses in ways that can distinguish grid avoidance from the ‘habitat fragmentation’, or small water body hypotheses.

Quantitative information is also needed about the degree to which aquatic insects associate with PV panels, especially at utility-scale facilities that are likely to

have a larger demographic impact on their populations. It’s known that the severity of the demographic impact of evolutionary traps is not just related to their relative attractiveness (Fletcher et al. 2012), but to their spatial location relative to population sources (Lerner et al. 2011; Robertson et al. 2018). Even in desert environments where natural water bodies are scarce, aquatic insects may be attracted to evolutionary traps (e.g. oil spills) where the nearest water body is over 50 miles distant (e.g. Horváth and Zeil 1996) and so knowledge of the spatial context and correlates of attraction (sensu Robertson et al. 2018) will also be a consideration in understanding where PV utility siting is likely to have demographic impacts on aquatic insect populations. Utility-scale solar installations are also responsible for the large-scale mortality of migratory birds (Walston et al. 2016). Birds are capable of visualizing polarized light (Muheim et al. 2016), too, may perceive solar panels as false water bodies, but might also be attracted to feed on the aquatic insects ‘trapped’ by polarizing PV panels. We recommend studies capable of testing among alternative sensory-cognitive mechanisms for attraction by both aquatic insects and birds, such that new panel designs may disarm evolutionary traps for these two groups, simultaneously.

Further development of our approach is necessary before it can be applicable as a mitigation strategy in a commercial setting, but our study contributes significantly to the growing breadth of work which suggests that the interplay between polarized and non-polarized light is an essential part of many insect behaviors. Notably, heterogeneous (striped, spotted) coat patterns of zebras and spotted mammals drastically reduce their visual attractiveness to blood-sucking biting flies, especially to tsetse flies and horseflies (Blahó et al. 2012, 2013; Egri et al. 2012; Horváth et al. 2014). This indicates that the strategies we are exploring to disguise solar panels from aquatic insects represent a broader strategy that has evolved many times independently among mammals seeking to hide themselves. More broadly, understanding of animal behavior is a key tool in conservation practice and wildlife management (Blumstein and Fernández-Juricic 2010) and our results indicate it will also play a key role in the development of an increasingly PV-powered energy grid that is compatible with wildlife conservation.
